lead: An electrode is the boundary where ion current in the body becomes electron current in a wire, through a double layer of separated charge at the metal surface. That layer adds a DC half-cell potential and an impedance of its own. Whether a millivolt ECG or a microvolt EEG reaches the amplifier cleanly depends on how well both are handled. This chapter covers the interface, its equivalent circuit, and the three families used in practice: surface, needle and microelectrodes.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for where the bio-potential comes from, and the idea of impedance as resistance and capacitance combined.

blocks.text: Nerve and muscle currents are carried by ions, mainly Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻, in salt water. Wires carry electrons. The electrode converts one into the other at its metal surface by a chemical reaction that gives an electron to an ion or takes one from it.

The reaction leaves electrons on the metal and a sheet of ions in the liquid just outside it. These opposite charge sheets form the double layer, which stores charge like a capacitor. Its steady voltage, measured against a standard hydrogen electrode, is the half-cell potential of that metal–electrolyte pair.

A recording uses two electrodes, each with its own half-cell potential. Their difference reaches the amplifier as an offset even when the tissue is silent. A matched pair gives a few millivolts; a mismatched pair gives tens to hundreds of millivolts, far more than a 1 mV ECG. This is the electrode offset potential.

When current flows, the half-cell potential shifts from equilibrium. That shift is polarisation, and a strongly polarised electrode drifts with current and time, ruining a long recording. Ag/AgCl in a chloride gel is almost non-polarisable: Ag ⇌ Ag⁺ + e⁻ reverses easily, so the offset stays small and steady. It is the standard for ECG, EEG and EMG. The Nernst equation relates ion concentration to this potential; only the name matters here.

Model one electrode as a DC source E_hc in series with a resistance R_s, shunted by a capacitance C_d and a leakage resistance R_d. R_s is the gel and skin path, often tens of kΩ on unprepared skin. C_d is the double layer and makes electrode impedance fall as frequency rises. R_d is the path by which charge crosses the interface through the reaction.

blocks.where: V_bio is the bio-potential generated by the tissue in volts; Z_e is the electrode impedance at that frequency in ohms; Z_in is the amplifier input impedance in ohms; V_in is the voltage actually present at the amplifier terminals.

blocks.text: To keep the loss under 1%, Z_in must be at least 100 times Z_e. A gelled surface electrode sits at a few kΩ, so a 1 MΩ input is plenty. A microelectrode at 10 MΩ needs 1 GΩ or more, which is why microelectrode amplifiers are built differently (see Chapter 1.4).

Two further points. Impedance is frequency dependent, so a mismatch shows up differently in the ECG and EEG bands. And the two electrodes of a differential pair should have equal impedance: unequal impedance turns 50 Hz mains pick-up from a common-mode voltage into a differential one the amplifier cannot reject. Abrade the skin and use matched electrodes.
Surface electrodes sit on the skin and record the summed activity of many cells below. Four shapes cover most clinical use.

items: Plate or disc: an Ag/AgCl snap on a foam pad with gel, pre-gelled and disposable, stuck on the chest for ECG.
Reusable plate: metal or rubber held by a strap; gel is applied each time and the electrode is cleaned between patients.
Suction: a metal cup pulled on by a rubber bulb; fast to attach on a limb or foetal scalp, easily dislodged.
Floating: the metal is recessed behind a gel column, so the double layer does not move when the metal or skin moves; motion artefact drops, which suits Holter and stress testing.

blocks.text: Disposable costs more per electrode but saves setup time and gives repeatable impedance. Reusable is cheaper per use, but the gel dries and the offset drifts over a long session.

Unipolar or bipolar. A unipolar arrangement uses one active electrode against a distant reference and sees a wide region. A bipolar arrangement uses two similar electrodes close together, sees a small region, and rejects what is common to both. Most ECG chest leads are unipolar against the Wilson terminal; limb leads I, II and III are bipolar pairs (see Chapter 1.5).

Needle electrodes pass through the skin into muscle. A monopolar needle is a fine stainless steel wire insulated except at the tip, used with a surface reference; the pickup region is wide. A concentric needle has a hollow cannula with a fine wire inside: wire active, cannula reference, so the pickup volume is small and sharp. Concentric needles record single motor units, which clinical EMG needs (see Chapter 1.6).

Microelectrodes record from one cell. A glass micropipette is a capillary pulled to a 0.1–1 µm tip and filled with 3 M KCl; current crosses the tip by ion movement, so tip resistance is high, roughly 10–100 MΩ, and a larger tip gives lower resistance. A metal microelectrode is tungsten or platinum–iridium etched to a point and insulated except at the tip; its resistance is about 1–10 MΩ, suited to extracellular spike recording.

High tip resistance costs bandwidth and signal. Tip resistance with cable capacitance forms a low-pass filter, and the divider above throws signal away unless Z_in is very large. Keep the lead short and put the first amplifier stage close to the electrode. Every electrode is also a conductive path into the body, and leakage current through an intracardiac electrode can cause microshock; limits and tests are in Unit 6, Electrical safety and testing.

examples.question: A glass microelectrode records a cell and has a tip resistance of 10 MΩ. The amplifier input impedance is 1 GΩ. What fraction of the bio-potential reaches the amplifier input, and what percentage is lost in the electrode?
steps: Write the data with units: Z_e = 10 MΩ = 10 × 10⁶ Ω and Z_in = 1 GΩ = 1 × 10⁹ Ω.
Electrode and input form a divider, V_in = V_bio × Z_in ÷ (Z_in + Z_e); the fraction arriving is Z_in ÷ (Z_in + Z_e).
The lost share is 1 − 0.9901 = 0.0099, that is 0.99%.
examples.answer: 0.9901 of the bio-potential (99.01%) reaches the amplifier and 0.99% is lost across the 10 MΩ tip resistance.
examples.check:
Z_e = 10e6
Z_in = 1e9
frac = Z_in / (Z_in + Z_e)
print(round(frac, 4))
print(round(frac * 100, 2))
print(round((1 - frac) * 100, 2))

traps: Do not treat the electrode offset as real bio-potential. It is a DC half-cell potential and must be blocked by the amplifier or cancelled by matched electrodes.
A good electrode does not have zero half-cell potential. Matching the two electrodes is what cancels it; a mismatched pair leaves a standing DC that can saturate the amplifier.
High electrode impedance also raises thermal noise and, if the two electrodes differ, converts common-mode mains into a differential voltage, so CMRR falls.
Microelectrode tip resistance is the pipette's own series resistance, not the cell membrane resistance. Candidates confuse the two in numerical problems.
Unipolar and bipolar describe the arrangement, not the shape. The same disc is unipolar in one lead and part of a bipolar pair in another; read which one the question describes.

quiz.q: Define half-cell potential and say what causes it.
quiz.a: The equilibrium DC voltage across the double layer at one metal–electrolyte interface, measured against a standard reference. It is caused by the charge-transfer reaction that leaves electrons on the metal and ions in the electrolyte.

quiz.q: Name the electrode material most used for surface bio-potential recording and the one property that makes it suitable.
quiz.a: Ag/AgCl. It is almost non-polarisable, so its half-cell potential stays small and stable when current flows.

quiz.q: Why does the impedance of a surface electrode fall as frequency rises?
quiz.a: The double layer acts as a capacitance C_d. Its reactance 1 ÷ (2πfC_d) falls as f rises, so the parallel C_d–R_d combination drops and total impedance falls.

quiz.q: Why must both electrodes of a differential pair use the same metal and the same gel?
quiz.a: Their half-cell potentials then nearly match and cancel at the amplifier input. Different metals give different potentials, so the difference appears as a DC offset that can saturate the amplifier.

quiz.q: A chest surface electrode has an impedance of 50 kΩ at the ECG band. The amplifier input impedance is 1 MΩ. What fraction of the bio-potential reaches the amplifier, and what percentage is lost?
quiz.a: Fraction = 1 × 10⁶ ÷ (1 × 10⁶ + 50 × 10³) = 0.9524. So 95.24% reaches the amplifier and 4.76% is lost.

quiz.q: A metal microelectrode has a tip resistance of 2 MΩ and is used with an amplifier of input impedance 100 MΩ. What fraction of the signal is lost?
quiz.a: Fraction reaching the amplifier = 100 ÷ (100 + 2) = 0.9804, that is 98.04%. The lost fraction is 0.0196, that is 1.96%.

quiz.q: A concentric needle records a smaller pickup volume than a monopolar needle. Explain why, using the idea of active and reference electrodes.
quiz.a: In a concentric needle the active wire and the cannula reference are micrometres apart on one shaft, so only fibres within a small radius contribute. In a monopolar needle the reference is a distant surface electrode, so the field spans a wide region and many fibres contribute.

quiz.q: A technician sees strong 50 Hz interference on an ECG although both electrodes are attached. The two electrode impedances differ by a factor of five. Explain how this produces interference and how to reduce it.
quiz.a: The mains voltage appears as a common-mode voltage on the body and divides across each electrode impedance and the amplifier input. Unequal impedances give unequal divider ratios, so part of the common-mode voltage appears differentially and is amplified as signal. Reduce it by abrading the skin, reapplying gel, choosing matched electrodes, and using a driven-right-leg circuit.

beyond: Not for the exam. Dry and capacitive electrodes are an active research direction: they avoid gel by sensing the field across a capacitive gap, and appear in wearable ECG patches and EEG headsets. Textile electrodes woven into clothing are used in smart shirts for continuous monitoring, and conductive-polymer coatings lower interface impedance without gel.
